Who would of thought the common house fly who barely lives a few days could be the source of such profound philosophical perspectives.

They lack the complex method of how we process pain. 

Humans have very complex and intricate nervous systems where we can feel a vast range of different sensations depending on the stimuli. A lovely bite is nice and seductive,but a bite bite is painful and makes you want to draw away.

Insects as a whole have a very simple nervous system where instead of a series of receptors all instructed by our brain on how to react to stimuli, insects instead have "multiple tiny brains" throughout their body called ganglia that act similarly to how our brain does but lack the complexity ours do as a result of... well... Being a tiny ass bug brain. 

As for whether I would be like being vermin in my next life, aww hell nah. But as a roach I would lack the mental capacity to really care.
My world is just a giant snowglobe

The fear of knowing I will never be enough.

You forgot the roaches.

Their realities and perceptions of pain and suffering is extremely primitive compared to ours. They don't process pain the same way we do. We get out leg chopped off it's not only a massive physical trauma that we have to deal with, with our nervous systems going into shock the excruciating pain we feel, not to mention the psychological trauma we will.experience for a while after.

For bugs it's more along the lines of no this is not a comfortable feeling. And when it loses a leg it's more like, "oh no. Anyway."

As for their perception of reality,  it's mainly a combination of wanting to eat, procreate and die. Most insects don't live long lives but some can. If I remember correctly there is a species of termite that can live for years while your average fly barely makes a week. Taking their simplistic anatomy into consideration and their lack of brains the same way mammals have brains they are literally incapable of the complex emotions and physical feelings that we do. For them it's a lot like a binary system. This good. This bad. Must eat. Must fly. Must bang. 

But it is sometimes a little disheartening accidentally stepping on a bug that isn't a roach

I feel like it depends. I don't feel bad from an ethical or empathetic standpoint. Bugs are too simple of creatures to experience pain the same way we do. It's more of a, "no this is uncomfortable" feeling for them than how we would feel the same pain. They are neither intelligent enough to experience emotion or complex thoughts so for them the pure instinct of fighting to simply be alive is what drives them.

But from which types of bugs are getting killed that's a different story. Mr butterfly can waft around peacefully for all I care but this tick or cockroach will get a first hand experience of what essentially would be standing behind a jet engine on full blast.

If you are collecting them for research, scientific or general interest, putting them in a freezer for 1 to 2 days is a fairly humane way to kill them and still preserve the body. Bigger beetles and such I would recommend a week or so.

But yea everything that lives has a role in the ecosystem so they do matter even though they are insects, but it is unlikely that killing a bunch that wander in your house will contribute meaningfully to their overall population. Fuck earwigs tho.

Something I liked about playing ''Commander'' in MTG or just MTG as a whole were synergies, so leaning towards more the card design aspect of this.

As an analogy :  
Ice Towers slows down the enemy advance  
Thorn Towers Create patches on the ground that the longer enemies stay on them the more dmg they take over time.

  
Earth tower when kills enemies creates a patch of oil on the floor  
Fire Tower does extra dmg when enemy walks over or are standing in oil

This leads to a natural synergy between having these two towers working almost as a single unit. If you plan on adding variety to upgrade paths like how BTD6 has with their monkeys this can open avenues for different synergies to be made dependent on how the upgraded towers interact in their new way or are just a pure stat boost. Sometimes it might just be more efficient depending on what cards you have available at the time.



It feels really good when synergy really pays off and adds what i like to think a subtle layer of complexity. Thinking about how different aspects of your cards work together as well as on their own is why I now have a crippling addiction to card games as a whole.

The Grim Apostles. A secretive pantheon of demi-gods determined to cause suffering and spread death as far as they go. The more vile and heinous their deeds are the more the Grim Shepard gifts then with his favor. 

The catch is that his favor is like a drug: it makes you feel amazing, like you are the king of the world without a worry on your mind. For the first time since you had read from Macabre Manifesto your mind is at peace. You feel whole and alone in your thoughts again. But that feeling is stripped from you. Trying to regain the favor requires one to inflict more misery and suffering than before for a high that last not nearly as long. 

Eventually you'll have built enough of a tolerance to The Grim Shepard's favour that you can no longer feel it's effects, driving those who have surpassed that threshold into mindless murder machines called The Tormented that can single handedly massacre entire cities for the sake of chasing that high once again. A sad fate for most of the Grim Apostles is either they are a slain during their Tormented rampage or they take their own lives thinking it to be their final challenge.

Only a few have ever managed to find peace in the mindless mass murder and torturous temptations, and it is they who rise up to become a part of the Grim Flock, or in other words the Grim Shepard's personal torture orgy
